## Part A — Creating Vectors: c(), seq(), rep()
```{r}
scores <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
subjects <- c("English", "History", "PE")

rep("A", times = 4)
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 2 )
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 2)
```
Question 1. Set up a vector named age, consisting of 15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8.

length(age)
1 / age

new_age <- c(age, 0, age)
min(age)

Question 2. rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) and rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) both produce a vector of length 4, but with different element orders.
Explain in your own words the difference between each and times.
```{r}
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 2)
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 2)
```
"each" repeasts each individual element consecutively the specified number before moving to the next element while "times" repeats the entire vector as single block.

Question 3. Compare seq(1, 20, by = 2) with seq(1, 20, length.out = 5). What does each argument (by vs length.out) control, and when would you use one over the other in a real analysis?
```{r}
seq(1, 20, by = 2)
seq(1, 20, length.out = 5)
```
"by" control the step size between consecutive numbers. while "length.out" control the total number of element in the output vector, automatically calculating equal spacing between the star and end values. I will use "by" when the fixed gap between data points is critical, I will use "length.out" when you need a fixed count of points across a range regardless of interval size

## Part B — Subsetting (Accessing) Vectors
```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")

grades[3]
grades[c(1, 4)]
grades[c("Science", "PE")]

grades[-c(1, 4)]
grades[grades >= 85]

grades[10]
```
Question 5. Negative indexing (grades[-1]) removes an element, while logical indexing (grades[grades >= 85]) filters by a condition.

Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.

use negative indexing when you want to remove the unwanted data points and use the logical indexing when you want to see who meets the condition.

Question 6. What happens if you run grades[10] (an index that doesn’t exist)? Run it, observe the result, and explain why R responds this way instead of throwing an error.

it returns <NA> NA R returns NA to signal missing data at this position.

Question 7. Print a vector with the integers between 1 and 100 that are not divisible by 3, 5 and 7 using filter option.
```{r}
Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3, 5, 7) != 0) }, seq(100))
```
## Part C — Vector Operations and append()
```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
x + y
x * y

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)
z + short

fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
append(fruits, "date")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)

z + c(1, 0, 1)
z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)
```
Question 8. In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.

Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

R's recycling rule automatically repeats the elements of the shorter vector from left to right until its length matches the longer vector.

Question 9. Now try adding z (length 6) to c(1, 0, 1) (length 3) instead. Does it work cleanly?

it executes cleanly without any warning message. R recycles c(1, 0, 1) exactly twice to match length 6.

Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.

if the length of the longer vector is not evenly divisible by the shorter length, R outputs a warning because the shorter vector had to be truncated mid-cycle to fit.

## Part D — Lists: Creating and Subsetting
```{r}
student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos",
  age = 20,
  grades = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)

student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])

student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])

student$name

student[["grades"]][2]
```
Question 10. student["grades"] and student[["grades"]] look similar but return objects of different classes.

Run class() on each and explain the difference in what single-bracket [ ] versus double-bracket [[ ]] return from a list.

Single brackets return a smaller sub list that still contains the requested element inside its list wrapper. while double brackets reach inside the list container and extract the underlying data object stored at that position.

Question 11. Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

A Vector is just a row of items of the exact same type, while list is a big box holding different data types.

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]

inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
```
Question 12. In challenge-1, you combined logical indexing on one vector (in_stock) to filter a different vector (item) inside the same list. Explain, step by step, why inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works even though item and in_stock are stored as separate elements of the list.

R first evaluates inventory$item to extract the vector c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser") and inventory$in_stock to extract the logical vector c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE). R relies on positional alignment. Even though they are separate vectors inside the list, index 1 in item ("Notebook") corresponds directly to index 1 in in_stock (TRUE), index 2 to TRUE, and index 3 to FALSE. R applies the logical vector as a filter mask: c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser")[c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)]. R retains every element at a TRUE position (index 1 and 2) and discards elements at a FALSE position (index 3), returning c("Notebook", "Pen").

Question 13. Suppose a classmate stores related data as three separate, unconnected vectors (item_names, item_prices, item_stock) instead of grouping them into one list like inventory. What risks or bugs could this create as the dataset grows or gets reordered? Argue for or against using a list (or, later, a data frame) instead of separate vectors.

Data Corruption if you sort, filter, or reorder item_names without applying the exact same operation in the exact same order to item_prices and item_stock, the alignment completely breaks. "Notebook" could suddenly be mapped to the price of "Eraser" ($5.00). And Length Mismatches if a function adds a value to item_names but forgets to update item_stock, the vectors become unequal in length. This leads to silent recycling errors or script crashes.

Conclusion: Vectors store a single data type like all numbers or all words, whereas lists act as containers that can hold various data types, lengths, and structures at the same time. Because lists wrap complex objects, vectors are accessed using simple single brackets [ ], while lists require double brackets [[ ]] or $ to unwrap and pull out the actual items inside. You should choose a vector when performing math operations or simple filtering on uniform data. In contrast, choose a list when bundling related attributes of different data types together into a single master object, like a student profile or store inventory.
